statement: In bodies examined after death, the measured concentration of a drug in blood can differ from the concentration at the moment of death, and from one blood vessel to another in the same body, by amounts that vary between drugs and between bodies and that, in the sources read, cannot yet be predicted for a given death. In four suspected overdose deaths chosen by forensic medicine authors in Dundee and Edmonton to illustrate the problem (tricyclic antidepressants, barbiturates and the sleeping medicine flurazepam; autopsy about 7 to 48 hours after death; office and period not stated), blood drawn separately from up to 11 vessels of the same body differed 3.5- to 6.6-fold for each drug taken in the overdose and 1.6-fold for lidocaine, given in hospital (editors' calculation from the printed ranges), usually highest in central vessels near the lungs and liver and lowest in the subclavian or femoral veins, though in one case the lowest value was in the pulmonary artery; in the only person with a blood sample from life, taken in hospital about one hour before cardiac arrest (the reported intervals imply about two hours before death), every post-mortem sample, femoral blood included, held 1.8 to 7.9 times as much imipramine (editors' calculation). The authors attribute the differences mainly to drug diffusing out of organs after death, while allowing incomplete distribution in life as a contributor and calling the cause unresolved and probably multifactorial; no body was sampled more than once and unabsorbed drug was still in the gut in three of the four, so part of the differences may have arisen before death (Pounder & Jones, 1990). A compilation of 10,993 results from 5,375 post-mortem cases for 50 compounds (published reports found by keyword searching, plus a Finnish national laboratory database for 2000 to 2018; cocaine, MDMA and cannabinoids were left out) calculated within-case ratios where a published source gave both values, then medians for each drug; the medians across these drug-specific medians were 1.27 for other blood such as heart blood (576 results), 0.99 for muscle, 0.45 for the fluid of the eye (vitreous humour), 1.84 for brain, 2.03 for heart muscle, 5.06 for liver and 5.52 for bile, with more than tenfold ranges across the available drug-specific medians in all ten specimen types (other blood from 0.90 to 14.61, vitreous humour from 0.03 to 1.59, liver from 0.95 to 54.29, some of these values resting on few results; for other blood, morphine 1.26 and methamphetamine 1.50); no within-drug range or interval is given, and cause of death and time since death, which the sources did not always give, could not be taken into account (Ketola & Kriikku, 2019). A review of 87 publications selected from a two-database search in April 2025 reports that in animal experiments drug levels in heart blood rose within minutes of death; that in human bodies sampled more than once, femoral blood, the sample thought least open to change (Ferner, 2008), rose significantly after death for about a dozen drugs, among them fentanyl and methadone, and fell for others, among them 6-MAM (the marker of heroin) and THC; and that, in the studies that reported or estimated it, the first sample was taken on average about 17 hours after death (range 1 to 292 hours), so change before then was not seen. It gives no sizes and does not appraise the studies; it judges that a heart-to-femoral blood ratio other than 1 can indicate, if the two were equal at death, that change after death occurred but not how much, and that a ratio of 1 does not rule it out, and it concludes that evidence linking the change to specific variables is often lacking, drug properties explaining only part of it (Borra et al., 2026). A 2003 practitioners' review lists 99 entries (98 distinct labels), of which 82 have numeric parentheses, including an ambiguous nicotine/cotinine annotation; two are ranges and 16 labels, including THC, have no numeric value. It gives no case counts or per-value source attribution (for example morphine 2.2, methamphetamine 2.4, MDMA 2.65, cocaine 1.5 to 2.3); for 17 of 24 shared labels its value exceeds 1.10 times the compilation's paired median for other blood. Other blood is not only heart blood, and the review's peripheral blood is not necessarily femoral; this comparison is descriptive, not a validated correction (editors' comparison; Leikin & Watson, 2003; Ketola & Kriikku, 2019), and a clinical pharmacologist's review adds that post-mortem whole blood is compared with plasma or serum values from living patients, and that the ratio between the two differs by drug even in life (Ferner, 2008). Change can run both ways: a level after death can be higher than in life, as in the one case with a hospital sample, which can make a drug look more involved in a death than it was, or it can fall after death, as reported for 6-MAM and THC, which can make a drug look less involved. The evidence consists of a selected case series, an unappraised compilation drawn mostly from published reports, some of them about poisonings, and narrative reviews, mostly about medicines; how often, and by how much, a level changes in an ordinary death is not known. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: Can the amount of a drug in the blood change after death? Yes. In four selected overdose deaths, levels in different blood vessels differed about 3 to 7 times for the drugs taken in overdose; a medicine given in hospital varied less. In one person tested in hospital before death, all later imipramine samples were about 2 to 8 times higher. A compilation found large differences between drugs and specimens. Its typical other-blood ratio was about a quarter above thigh blood, but that was a median across drug-specific medians, not an average of all deaths. Repeated tests after death found rises for some drugs and falls for others. The size and frequency of these changes in ordinary deaths remain unknown.
magnitude: Within one body (four selected overdoses, autopsy about 7 to 48 h after death): highest to lowest blood value 3.5- to 6.6-fold per drug taken in the overdose (editors' calculation; doxepin 3.5, amobarbital 6.0, secobarbital 6.5, pentobarbital 6.2, clomipramine 5.4, flurazepam 6.6, imipramine 4.4; lidocaine given in hospital 1.6). One case with a sample from life: post-mortem imipramine 4.1–18.1 mg/L against 2.3 mg/L in hospital, 1.8- to 7.9-fold. Medians across drug-specific medians of paired within-case ratios (printed number of results): other blood 1.27 (576), muscle 0.99 (385), vitreous humour 0.45 (356), brain 1.84 (565), heart 2.03 (185), kidney 2.86 (401), lung 3.69 (187), spleen 4.25 (71), liver 5.06 (1,697), bile 5.52 (537); between drugs, liver 0.95–54.29, vitreous 0.03–1.59, other blood 0.90–14.61; other blood for morphine 1.26 (53), methamphetamine 1.50 (9). Human repeated sampling: first sample on average 17 h after death (range 1–292 h) where reported or estimated; rises in femoral blood for about 12 drugs, falls for 5 (no sizes). Narrative-review approximate heart-to-peripheral values without case counts or per-value sources (82 numeric-labelled entries among 98 distinct labels, including a nicotine/cotinine annotation; two ranges): morphine 2.2, methamphetamine 2.4, MDMA 2.65, cocaine 1.5–2.3; more than 10% above the compilation's paired other-blood median for 17 of 24 drugs in both (editors' comparison). No within-drug intervals are given. The Table 3 N columns sum to 4,960 but include one oxazepam brain count without a printed ratio; the counts are results, not distinct deaths.

risk_of_bias.note: The site differences come from four overdose deaths chosen to illustrate the problem, with no denominator and no serial sampling (card sc_pounder_1990, JBI high); the ratios come from a compilation drawn mostly from published reports, some of them focused on poisonings, without study-level appraisal or uncertainty estimates (its number-weighted descriptive summaries do not supply study-level precision weighting or within-drug spread) (card sc_ketola_2019, AMSTAR 2 by analogy, critically low); the changes over time are relayed without sizes from a review that does not appraise its studies (card sc_borra_2026). Selection of striking cases could make the differences look larger than in ordinary deaths.

inconsistency.note: Not downgraded: every source points the same way (levels differ by site and change after death); the size varies by drug, which the claim states rather than hides.

indirectness.note: The question concerns deaths involving any drug, including drugs used outside medicine; the compilation excludes cocaine, MDMA and cannabinoids, the case series concerns large overdoses of medicines with drug still in the gut, and part of the evidence on timing is from animals.

imprecision.note: Four cases; no ranges, percentiles or intervals for any compiled ratio; many drug–specimen ratios rest on one to three results.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable for case series and compilations of case literature.

grade.reasoning: A descriptive claim starts low and is never upgraded (METHODS §6.3); down for risk of bias, indirectness and imprecision, which reaches the floor: very low. Strict reading: that drug levels can differ between sampling sites and change after death is shown consistently by independent designs (a case series with a sample from life, a large compilation of paired values, repeated-sampling studies as reviewed) and on its own would be rated low; the sizes, and how often a change matters in an ordinary death, are very low. Status replicated: Pounder & Jones and the primary studies compiled by Ketola & Kriikku and reviewed by Borra et al. are independent and agree in direction. Counted once: Pounder & Jones is one of the compilation's doxepin sources; Ferner (2008) takes its heart-to-femoral ratios from Leikin & Watson (2003), so the narrative reviews' ratios are one source, used only as second-hand examples.

statement: A drug concentration measured after death cannot on its own show that the drug caused the death: concentrations in deaths put down to a drug overlap with those in deaths from other causes and with the reference ranges of living patients taking the drug as a treatment, tolerance shifts the level a person can survive, and levels change after death (see the answer on whether levels change after death). In Finland, where police can order a medico-legal investigation of a sudden or unexplained death and the forensic pathologist decides whether to test for drugs (over 13% of all deaths), one laboratory measured femoral-blood levels in 57,903 deaths of all causes with full drug testing in 2000 to 2010, sampled on average five days after death; for 46 of 129 drugs the median level was above the therapeutic plasma range of a clinical reference list, by up to 100-fold for one drug (24-fold for the next), for 61 it was within that range and for 22 below it. The median for methadone (207 deaths) and for buprenorphine (671 deaths) lay within the treatment range although forensic pathologists certified 43% and 45% of those deaths as poisonings with that drug as the main finding, and the authors state that for strong opioids the level after death plays a somewhat limited part in judging the cause, as it partly does for amphetamine and other drugs to which tolerance develops; the medians mix poisonings with other deaths, leave out levels too low to measure, and compare whole blood with plasma ranges (Launiainen & Ojanperä, 2014). Among deaths with MDMA or a related drug found at full autopsy in Sheffield, England (1992 to 2008), femoral-blood MDMA overlapped widely between deaths put down to MDMA (0.478 to 53.9 mg/L in 13 with a value) and deaths from injuries (0.035 to 4.81 mg/L in 24), although the median was about 7 times higher in the first group (editors' calculation; Milroy, 2011; see the answer on MDMA levels). A Michigan series published in 1977, as the 1996 narrative review describes it, found blood morphine no higher than in people who used heroin and died of other causes, such as injuries or homicide, in 74% of deaths put down to heroin overdose (Darke & Zador, 1996, second-hand; see the answer on heroin 'overdoses'). A clinical pharmacologist's review adds, second-hand, that published 'lethal' ranges are wide and overlap (for example 40 to 8,500 µg/L quoted for MDMA and 60 to 3,100 µg/L for methadone), that amounts that would kill a person without tolerance are survived by people who use heroin regularly, and that a fatal level could only be defined by classing deaths as caused by the drug or not without knowing the measured levels and then comparing the two groups (Ferner, 2008), which none of the studies read here reports doing; a 2003 practitioners' review lists nine questions a toxicologist should answer before judging a drug's role, among them where the blood was taken, whether the drug changes after death, what is known of the person's tolerance and whether the autopsy findings fit (Leikin & Watson, 2003). Both directions follow: a level that looks high can lead to a death being put down to a drug that was only present, and an ordinary or low level does not rule a drug out. A study of whether drugs were present, not of their levels, shows that judging without a full autopsy also errs both ways: at one North Carolina centre that kept doing full autopsies on suspected drug deaths (2016 to 2021), 265 of 2,719 deaths that investigators suspected before autopsy to be drug deaths (9.75%) were given a final cause unrelated to drugs after full autopsy and toxicology (by the paper's definition, deaths with no drug found or with drugs present but another sufficient cause; the split is not reported; people under 18, obvious lethal injuries and suicidal drug overdoses were excluded), while 115 of the 237 deaths not suspected (48.5%, editors' calculation) were judged drug deaths; the pathologists counted any illicit drug found as at least contributing unless a catastrophic other cause was found (Hancock et al., 2024; see the answer on autopsy and toxicology testing). The earlier source extraction reports that the Finnish certifiers received the toxicology results; in the North Carolina study the final cause followed full autopsy and toxicology; the Sheffield and Michigan reports, as read here, do not say who decided the causes or whether the levels were known. None of the studies read here itself compares post-mortem levels with levels in living people who use the drugs outside treatment; the heroin review cites three comparisons with survivors of overdose, without figures. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: Can a blood test after death show that a drug caused the death? Not on its own. In an English autopsy study, MDMA levels in deaths put down to MDMA overlapped with levels in people who died of injuries. A review reports similar findings for morphine in an older US study. Finnish data compare levels after death with treatment reference ranges, rather than testing living patients in the same study. At one US centre, full autopsy and toxicology led to a different final classification in both directions: some suspected drug deaths were judged unrelated to drugs, and some unsuspected deaths were judged drug-related. That study examined drug presence, not blood levels. The certifiers' knowledge and rules limit what these comparisons can show.
magnitude: Finland 2000–2010 (57,903 deaths; 129 drugs): median femoral concentration above the therapeutic plasma range for 46 drugs (printed 35%; 35.7%, editors' calculation), within for 61 (47%), below for 22 (17%); the older card proposes 48, 58 and 23 under a consistent rule, but that source-table reconstruction was not independently repeated by reader 405; largest ratio to the upper therapeutic limit 100 (hydroxychloroquine), next 24 (promazine). Methadone median 0.40 mg/L (therapeutic 0.1–0.5), 43% certified as poisonings with methadone as the main finding; buprenorphine 0.0012 mg/L (0.0005–0.005), 45%; morphine 0.07 mg/L (0.01–0.1), 4%. Sheffield 1992–2008: MDMA deaths 0.478–53.9 mg/L (median 3.49; n = 13), injury deaths 0.035–4.81 mg/L (median 0.483; n = 24); at least 7 of the 13 inside the injury range (editors' calculation). Michigan series published in 1977 (study years unstated; second-hand): 74% of heroin overdose deaths with morphine no higher than in people who used heroin and died of other causes. Quoted lethal ranges (second-hand): MDMA 40–8,500 µg/L, methadone 60–3,100 µg/L. North Carolina 2016–2021 (presence, not levels): 265/2,719 (9.75%) suspected drug deaths with a non-drug final cause; 115/237 (48.5%, editors' calculation) of deaths not suspected judged drug deaths. No intervals.

risk_of_bias.note: In Finland and North Carolina the causes of death were assigned by forensic pathologists who had the case's toxicology results, and the Sheffield and Michigan reports do not say who assigned them or what was known, which can build part of any difference between groups into the comparison; the Finnish medians mix poisonings with other deaths and leave out levels too low to measure (card sc_launiainen_2014, JBI moderate); the MDMA groups are small and their certifiers unnamed (card sc_milroy_2011, JBI high); the heroin figure is second-hand; the North Carolina reference standard counts illicit drugs present as contributing (card sc_hancock_2024, JBI moderate).

inconsistency.note: Not downgraded: the medicine registry, the MDMA series and the heroin series all show overlap between levels in deaths put down to a drug and in other people or deaths.

indirectness.note: No study compares post-mortem levels with levels in living people who use the drugs outside treatment: the living comparison is plasma ranges from treatment, measured in a different body fluid; the large registry is about medicines in one country, and the heroin and lethal-range figures are second-hand.

imprecision.note: Not downgraded for the registry (57,903 deaths); the MDMA and heroin series are small but are used for the direction of the overlap, not its size.

grade.reasoning: A descriptive claim starts low and is never upgraded (METHODS §6.3); down for risk of bias and indirectness: very low. Status replicated: the Finnish registry and the Sheffield series are independent primary studies that agree in direction, and the 1977 heroin series, known here only through Darke & Zador, points the same way. The narrative reviews (Ferner; Leikin & Watson) supply the argument and examples, not data, and are labelled second-hand. The North Carolina study concerns autopsy, not levels, and is cited only for deaths put down to a drug that was present but did not cause the death; it is the subject of the answer on autopsy and toxicology testing and is not counted as replication here.

statement: Evidence is insufficient to say whether cannabis use causes sudden deaths from heart or blood-vessel problems, and the Finnish autopsy table cited here reports 0%, rounded to whole percent, as fatal poisonings with THC (the main active substance of cannabis) as the main finding. This is not an exact count of zero, does not cover every possible contribution, and is not a worldwide mortality rate. A 2019 narrative review by three forensic medicine authors in Victoria, Australia (English-language reports found in two databases, with broad inclusion rules but no search dates, screening counts or study-level appraisal) counted six publications describing 13 deaths, all of men aged 17 to 52, that the case authors, and in one case a coroner, linked to recent cannabis use: 8 of the 13 had significant coronary artery disease or other pathology, THC was measured in blood in 8 (1.9 to 22 ng/mL), the other 5 rested on urine tests or the person's history (in one of them no THC was found in blood, yet the coroner found cannabis a secondary cause), alcohol was found in 2, two died days after reaching hospital and one had no autopsy (Drummer et al., 2019). The reviewers write that the larger studies and systematic reviews leave the link between cannabis use and death from heart disease unclear and the risk probably rare, that it may not be possible to give a minimum causal blood THC level because of delays between death and sampling (most laboratories detect 1 to 2 ng/mL, and lower values may reflect use days earlier), and that a blood THC test, not urine or history alone, is needed to link a death to recent use; yet they recommend that, with very recent use, a positive blood THC and a possible heart or brain-vessel cause, cannabis be considered at least a contributory cause of a sudden death, that THC be recorded in death statistics, and they call the 13 deaths 'very likely to be an under-estimate of the true incidence', without data on how many deaths are missed (Drummer et al., 2019). The review also notes, without details or numbers, that some deaths have been attributed to cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome (severe repeated vomiting; four references, not read here; Drummer et al., 2019). They relay, second-hand, studies pointing both ways: a heart-attack risk 4.8 times the baseline (95% CI 2.9 to 9.5) in the first hour after smoking cannabis, as the review relays it (the primary interval was not checked), in a case-crossover study of 3,882 people, and a higher death rate after a heart attack with weekly use (hazard ratio 4.2, 1.2 to 14, in 1,913 people), against no association with cardiovascular death in 5,113 young US adults followed for more than 25 years and no increase in overall in-hospital mortality in more than two million US heart-attack admissions, and two systematic reviews that disagree; the review's statement that eleven of its twelve tabulated studies showed raised risk is not borne out by its own table (Drummer et al., 2019). In Finland, among 57,903 medico-legal autopsies with full drug testing in 2000 to 2010, THC was found in femoral blood in 347 deaths (median 0.002 mg/L, that is 2 ng/mL), and the table prints 0% certified as fatal poisonings with THC as the main finding. One of 347 would also round to 0% under ordinary rounding, so the exact count is not established by that percentage alone (Launiainen & Ojanperä, 2014). THC levels after death are hard to read: THC in femoral blood fell between repeated samples after death in one study, while other before/after comparisons reported higher THC after death than in samples from life; the comparisons have different timing and possible matrix differences and do not isolate redistribution from every other process (Borra et al., 2026, second-hand, without effect sizes), and a review gives a factor of 1.6 for calculating plasma cannabinoid concentrations from whole blood, without validating it for every post-mortem THC case (Leikin & Watson, 2003, second-hand). The case reports have no comparison group and cannot show how often THC is present in sudden deaths that cannabis did not cause, so these reports cannot validate the reviewers' attribution rule or an undercount estimate. Their criteria include excluding other reasonable explanations and considering a plausible mechanism as well as THC and the circumstances. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
plain: Can cannabis cause a sudden death? The evidence read here does not settle this. A review collected 13 deaths linked to recent use, all in men; 8 had significant heart disease or other illness, alcohol was found in 2, and 5 lacked a blood THC result showing recent use. Some died days after hospital admission. The reports have no comparison group. Larger studies, known here through the review, point both ways for heart attacks and death; some found no increased mortality. The Finnish table prints 0% as poisonings mainly attributed to THC, rounded to whole percent; it does not give an exact zero count or settle other forms of contribution. The reviewers encourage counting cannabis as a contributor in appropriate cases but give no estimate of missed deaths. Certainty remains very low.
magnitude: Not estimable as a risk. Case reports (Drummer et al., 2019): 13 deaths, men aged 17–52 (median 37); coronary disease or other pathology 8/13; blood THC measured in 8 (1.9–22 ng/mL), urine or history only in 5 (one blood-negative); alcohol in 2 (0.04% and 0.119%). Relayed: acute myocardial infarction 4.8 (95% CI 2.9–9.5) in the first hour after smoking, as relayed (primary interval unread); 1.7 (0.6–5.1) in the second hour in the text, labelled within 2 h in Table 3 (case-crossover, n = 3,882); mortality after MI, HR 4.2 (1.2–14) weekly use, 2.5 (0.9–7.3) less than weekly (n = 1,913); CARDIA (n = 5,113, over 25 years): no association with cardiovascular mortality. Desai summary: no increase in overall mortality in over two million AMI admissions, despite a separate AMI association. Finland 2000–2010: THC in femoral blood in 347 deaths, median 0.002 mg/L, 97.5th percentile 0.024 mg/L, 0% certified as fatal poisoning with THC as the main finding, rounded to whole percent; no exact zero count established. These Finnish values are inherited checked anchors, not freshly verified against the unavailable primary by reader 405.

risk_of_bias.note: The deaths are published case reports, chosen by their authors for a suspected link and not appraised by the review (card sc_drummer_2019, editors' checklist high); certification in the registry rests on pathologists' judgment without stated criteria (card sc_launiainen_2014).

inconsistency.note: The epidemiological studies relayed point in different directions (raised heart-attack risk in the hour after use and higher death rates after a heart attack, against no association with cardiovascular death in a 25-year cohort and a systematic review finding no compelling link with mortality). The review also relays a null overall-mortality result in over two million AMI admissions; AMI association and mortality are separate outcomes.

indirectness.note: The epidemiology is known only through a narrative review and mostly concerns heart attack and stroke, not death; the case reports span decades and several countries; five of the 13 deaths lack the blood test the reviewers themselves require.

imprecision.note: Thirteen deaths with no denominator or comparison group; no estimate of a death risk exists in the sources read.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable; case reports are published because a link was suspected, which the risk-of-bias rating covers.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low; down for risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness and imprecision, which is below the floor: very low. Status contested: the forensic reviewers' recommendation to count cannabis as a contributory cause and their view that such deaths are undercounted meet their own statement that the link is unclear, a 25-year cohort with no association and a registry table giving a rounded 0% for poisoning with THC as the main finding among 347 THC-positive deaths, which neither establishes an exact zero nor covers all contribution; the six-part debate box applies. The two systematic reviews and the cohort studies are known only through Drummer et al. and are not counted as replication. The claim gives no advice and makes no statement about amounts.
